The first cholera pandemic, which began in 1817 near Calcutta in the Ganges delta and spread across Asia and as far as the Mediterranean before dying out in 1824. Millions died.

Cholera had long been present in Bengal and had broken out in India many times before. This outbreak went much further. It spread along the new routes of British rule and trade: with British and Indian troops on campaign, with ships, and with pilgrims.

Where it went:

  • across India, and to Ceylon and Burma,
  • east to Siam and Java, to China, and to Japan in 1822,
  • west by sea to Oman, the Persian Gulf and Basra, then into Persia, Syria and Anatolia,
  • north to the Caspian Sea, reaching Russian Astrakhan in 1823,
  • south along the coast of East Africa.

About 10,000 British soldiers died, which drew European attention. The disease seems to have faded in the hard winter of 1823 to 1824.

It was the first of a series. The second pandemic, from 1826, reached Europe and North America and terrified their cities. No one then knew the cause. In 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to a single water pump, and in 1883 Robert Koch identified the bacterium. Cholera spreads through water fouled by sewage, and the fear it caused drove the building of clean water supplies and sewers in the 19th century.
sum: The first cholera pandemic, which began in 1817 near Calcutta in the Ganges delta and spread across Asia and as far as the Mediterranean before dying out in 1824. Millions died.
